canonical_statement: The study investigates whether training an LLM policy against a single frozen LLM user simulator causes poor generalization and evaluates inference-time and training-time interventions intended to prevent this failure.
The authors define simulator collapse on training rollouts as low expected probability of the simulator deviating from its modal response at the simulator turns visited by the current policy.

The authors hypothesize that a mode-collapsed simulator turns multi-agent RL into a fixed-user setting in which the policy learns a simulator-specific exploit that fails when unseen models or real users deviate from the simulator mode.

Multi-turn dialogue is modeled as a two-player POMDP or related stochastic-game abstraction in which the simulator affects the state-visitation distribution as well as the reward-bearing trajectories.
The agent policy is updated with REINFORCE-style full-trajectory training using group-relative z-scored terminal rewards, with zero within-group reward variance yielding no update.

Theorem 3.2 states that when accumulated simulator collapse error is small, the policy gradient under the simulator is close to the gradient under a deterministic mode-user environment, with norm gap bounded by 2 B Rmax times the accumulated collapse error.
Lemma 3.3 states that simulator collapse removes simulator-side reward contrast by upper-bounding simulator-side reward variance by Rmax squared times the trajectory collapse error.

Proposition 3.4 and Corollary 3.5 provide a sufficient mechanism under an idealized KL-regularized softmax update by which a persistent advantage for simulator-mode exploit strategies geometrically concentrates policy mass on those strategies.

Proposition 3.6 states conditions under which concentration on simulator-mode exploit strategies produces positive deployment regret when real users exhibit behaviors requiring strategies outside the exploit set.
The policy-concentration argument is a stylized strategy-level model rather than a direct theorem about the implemented token-level GRPO-style optimizer.
Across single-simulator runs against GPT-5-mini, Haiku-4.5, and Gemini-3-Flash, training reward rises while held-out evaluation peaks and then declines and policy entropy falls toward zero.
Verbalized Sampling queries the frozen simulator for multiple plausible responses with verbalized probabilities at each simulator turn and samples one response from that distribution.

Proposition 3.7 states that if the Verbalized Sampling distribution is close in total variation to a reference user distribution along visited states, its policy gradient is correspondingly close to the reference-user gradient.
The reference-recovery assumption for Verbalized Sampling is empirical and does not establish closeness between the reference distribution and real users.
Co-Training updates the simulator on its turns of the same conversations used to update the policy so that the simulator mode changes as training proceeds.
Population Co-Training samples the active simulator from a FIFO pool of recent simulator checkpoints rather than using only the latest simulator.
The evaluation covers three multi-turn benchmarks: Persuasion for Good, tau-squared-bench, and CooperBench.

population.label: Three multi-turn benchmark families: Persuasion for Good, tau-squared-bench, and CooperBench

canonical_statement: Persuasion for Good uses a donation-based adversarial dialogue reward defined as min(donation/2, 1).

Tau-squared-bench uses retail and airline customer-service dialogues with binary per-split success, and the trainable simulator uses a SPICE-style curriculum reward targeting within-batch variance near 0.25.
CooperBench uses two coding agents with shared binary task-success reward; Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.5-27B are used because smaller models could not complete the tasks.
P4G and tau-squared-bench are evaluated every 16 training steps on a six-simulator panel spanning three training-model families and three evaluation-only families.
Checkpoint selection uses the full six-simulator panel mean, which leaks partial training-simulator signal into model selection.
Headline method comparisons are matched on optimizer-step count rather than compute; frozen-simulator methods update only the agent, whereas Co-Training methods update both agent and simulator.
On P4G with Qwen3-4B-Instruct, RL (Single) achieved best held-out reward 0.275 versus Base 0.216.

canonical_statement: Best-checkpoint values for RL (Single) can represent transient peaks: on tau-squared-bench the policy later falls back toward the untrained baseline while population methods remain at or above their peak.
On CooperBench with Qwen3.5-9B, Population self-play achieved 33.6% held-out success versus 28.8% for fixed Haiku cross-play and 23.7% for Base.
On CooperBench with Qwen3.5-27B, Population self-play achieved 62.4% held-out success versus 54.3% for fixed Haiku cross-play and 47.8% for Base.

In CooperBench training curves, fixed-partner cross-play shows conversation turns rising and then falling as a shorter exploit strategy takes over, whereas self-play and Population Co-Training avoid this regression.
The human study evaluates Base, RL (Single), Verbalized Sampling, and Co-Training on tau-squared-bench and P4G using Qwen3-4B-Instruct policies.
The human study includes 320 Prolific sessions: four conditions across two tasks with N=40 participants per condition-task cell.

population.label: Prolific participants across four policy conditions and two tasks

canonical_statement: Human-study recruitment required English as a first language, Prolific approval rate at least 95%, at least 50 prior submissions, residence in one of six English-native countries, and desktop-device participation.

population.label: Human-study Prolific participants
inclusion_criteria: Residence in US, UK, Canada, Ireland, Australia, or New Zealand

canonical_statement: Condition assignment was server-side using the least-populated slot with hash-based tie-breaking on Prolific ID, keeping cells within plus or minus one session.
The pre-registered primary outcomes were tau-squared-bench task reward and P4G intended donation; secondary outcomes included survey items and three derived transcript measures.

Per-condition means were reported with 95% bootstrap percentile confidence intervals from 10,000 resamples; pre-registered pairwise tests used Welch t tests or Fisher exact tests with Holm-Bonferroni correction within panels.
In the tau-squared-bench human study, task outcome was 0.43 for RL (Single), 0.63 for Verbalized Sampling, and 0.70 for Co-Training; both interventions were marked p<0.01 versus RL (Single).

population.label: Tau-squared-bench Prolific participants, N=40 per condition

population.label: Persuasion for Good Prolific participants, N=40 per condition

canonical_statement: P4G dialogue naturalness in the human study was 3.21 for RL (Single), 4.33 for Verbalized Sampling, and 4.45 for Co-Training; both interventions were marked p<0.01 versus RL (Single).

canonical_statement: The human-study protocol had institutional IRB approval, and infrastructure-fault interruptions were paid in full regardless of completion.
Survey instruments, recruitment materials, and anonymized human-study response data are reported as available in the supplementary materials.
The pre-registered adversarial tau-squared-bench subgroup had approximately 12 participants per cell and was reported with explicit power caveats.

In the checkpoint-pool sweep K in {1,3,5,10}, K=5 performed best asymptotically, followed by K=10, K=3, and K=1; the authors attribute the interior optimum to stale checkpoints diluting useful variation.

On tau-squared-bench Retail, adversarial and cooperative simulator rewards both caused the trainable simulator to collapse to new dominant modes, while the variance-targeting curriculum preserved useful variation.
With the adversarial simulator reward on tau-squared-bench Retail, the simulator reached approximately 98% refusal and held-out eval reward fell to 0.07.
With the cooperative simulator reward on tau-squared-bench Retail, pushback fell to approximately 2% and held-out eval reward fell from 0.27 to 0.17.
The curriculum simulator reward kept opponent reward near 0.45 and reached approximately 0.40 held-out eval reward, outperforming the no-co-training ensemble baseline in the reward ablation.
In full tau-squared-bench Retail diagnostics, single-simulator RL zero-variance batches rose from about 60% to over 85%.
In full tau-squared-bench Retail diagnostics, single-simulator RL policy entropy fell from about 1.9 to 0.4 nats.
In full tau-squared-bench Retail diagnostics, all-failure batches under single-simulator RL rose to about 70%.

Scaling the trainable policy from Qwen3-4B-Instruct to Qwen3-8B did not eliminate the simulator-collapse pattern; the larger model appeared to collapse later but showed the same qualitative training-reward, OOD-eval, and entropy behavior.
Against GPT-5-mini, Verbalized Sampling maintained policy entropy near 0.7-0.8 nats while RL (Single) collapsed near zero.

quantitative_result.original_result_text: VS near 0.7-0.8 nats; RL Single near zero

canonical_statement: Against GPT-5, Verbalized Sampling ended near 0.70 held-out OOD reward while RL (Single) peaked near 0.65-0.67 and then degraded.

quantitative_result.original_result_text: RL Single peaks ~0.65-0.67 and degrades; VS ends near 0.70

canonical_statement: Replicating P4G and tau-squared-bench Retail with Olmo-3-7B-Instruct reproduced the same collapse-and-recovery ordering despite different initial entropy and base performance.
SCOPE provides one pluggable opponent-generation interface covering frozen heterogeneous simulator rotation, self-play or dual-model Co-Training, historical checkpoint pools, and Verbalized Sampling.
The training loop uses 250 steps, 16 prompts per rollout batch, 8 samples per prompt, global batch size 128, rollout temperature 0.7, and group-relative advantage normalization.
Maximum user/agent interaction horizons are 10 turns for P4G, 30 for tau-squared-bench, and 50 for CooperBench, with 64,000-token maximum context length.

For Qwen3-4B on tau-squared-bench Retail, approximate wall-clock time per step was 250 seconds for RL (Single), 280 seconds for Verbalized Sampling, and 500 seconds for Co-Training or Population Co-Training.

quantitative_result.original_result_text: ~250 s RL Single; ~280 s VS; ~500 s Co-Training/Population Co-Training

canonical_statement: Approximate total GPU-hours for a 250-step tau-squared-bench Retail run were 280 for RL (Single) and 560 for Co-Training or Population Co-Training.
The paper does not report an iso-compute sweep; the headline experiments isolate the training-environment intervention at matched step count.
The fixed simulator pool is limited by the diversity of the chosen models and remains fixed during training; adaptive pool curation is left for future work.
The held-out evaluator panel consists of aligned LLMs and may share RLHF-induced biases with the training simulators; the human study is the direct test of real-user transfer.
Co-Training depends on task-specific simulator reward shaping that preserves cross-checkpoint variation, and the authors have not mapped the broader space of rewards that would work.
Both interventions add compute overhead over single-simulator RL, particularly Co-Training because both sides are updated.

All three evaluated settings are text-only, two-agent, English, and substantially LLM-panel evaluated; extension to N-agent populations, multimodal environments, and non-English settings remains open.

The authors conclude that simulator diversity is a critical determinant of multi-turn RL generalization and that training against a single frozen mode-collapsed simulator can induce low-entropy simulator-specific policy behavior.
The authors report releasing SCOPE as an open-source framework for population-based multi-agent reinforcement learning.
